chapter.name: Gravitation
chapter.blurb: The chapter states Kepler's three laws of planetary motion and Newton's universal law of gravitation, and describes how Cavendish measured the gravitational constant. It then finds the acceleration due to gravity at, above and below the earth's surface, and introduces gravitational potential energy and potential with their zero at infinity. Finally it uses energy conservation to obtain the escape speed and treats earth satellites in circular orbits: their speed, period and energy.

scope_in.item: State Kepler's laws of orbits, areas and periods; describe an ellipse by its foci, perihelion, aphelion and semi-major axis; use T^2 proportional to a^3 to compare periods and orbit sizes (including the data of Table 7.1)

Explain the law of areas as a consequence of conservation of angular momentum under a central force (area swept per unit time = L/2m) and relate speeds and distances at perihelion and aphelion (Example 7.1)

State the universal law of gravitation for point masses, F = G m1 m2 / r^2, its attractive and equal-and-opposite character, and Newton's moon argument (g/a_m about 3600); calculate the force between two point masses
Find the resultant gravitational force on a point mass due to several point masses by vector addition (superposition), including symmetric arrangements (Example 7.2)
Describe Cavendish's torsion-balance experiment, equate the gravitational torque to the restoring torque (G M m L / d^2 = tau theta) and quote G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2

State and use the two results for a uniform spherical shell (outside point: mass as if at the centre; inside point: zero force) and apply them to the earth treated as concentric shells, including the force on a mass inside a uniform earth
Derive and use g = G M_E / R_E^2 at the earth's surface, its independence of the body's mass, and the estimate of the earth's mass M_E = g R_E^2 / G
Calculate g at a height h, exactly as G M_E / (R_E + h)^2 and for small h as g(1 - 2h/R_E), and at a depth d in a uniform earth as g(1 - d/R_E); state that g is greatest at the surface
Explain gravitational potential energy as arising from a conservative force; use mgh near the surface and -G M m / r (zero at infinity) at arbitrary distance; find differences of potential energy
Find the potential energy of a system of particles as a sum over all pairs, and the gravitational potential (potential energy per unit mass, -G M / r, in J/kg) at a point (Example 7.3)

Derive the escape speed from conservation of energy, sqrt(2 G M_E / R_E) = sqrt(2 g R_E), about 11.2 km/s for the earth and 2.3 km/s for the moon; apply energy conservation to projection problems, including the neutral point between two fixed spheres (Example 7.4)

For a satellite in a circular orbit, equate gravitational and centripetal force to get V^2 = G M_E / (R_E + h) and T^2 = k (R_E + h)^3 with k = 4 pi^2 / (G M_E); find T_0 = 2 pi sqrt(R_E / g), about 85 minutes; find the mass of a central body from an orbit (Examples 7.5-7.7)

Write the kinetic, potential and total energy of a satellite in a circular orbit (E = -G m M_E / 2(R_E + h)), explain why the total energy of a bound satellite is negative, and calculate the energy needed to change orbit or to escape (Example 7.8)

concepts.name: Kepler's laws of planetary motion
concepts.description: The laws of orbits, areas and periods for planets round the Sun, the ellipse and its foci and semi-major axis, and the law of areas as a consequence of the conservation of angular momentum under a central force.
concepts.idea: Planets move round the Sun in ellipses, not circles, and three simple laws found by Kepler from Tycho Brahe's observations describe the shape of the orbit, how the speed changes along it and how the period grows with the size of the orbit.
concepts.rule: Law of orbits: all planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun situated at one of the foci. For any point on an ellipse the sum of the distances from the two foci is constant; the closest point to the Sun is the perihelion, the farthest is the aphelion, and the semi-major axis is half the distance between them. A circle is the special case in which the two foci merge. Law of areas: the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal intervals of time, so the planet is slower when farther from the Sun. This follows from conservation of angular momentum, valid for any central force: area swept per unit time = L/(2m). At perihelion and aphelion the velocity is perpendicular to the Sun-planet line, so r_p v_p = r_a v_a. Law of periods: the square of the time period of revolution is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis, T^2 proportional to a^3.
concepts.example: A planet whose semi-major axis is 25 times that of the earth has T^2 = 25^3 = 15625 (in year^2), so T = 125 years.

Its distance from the Sun is 2 AU at perihelion and 6 AU at aphelion, where 1 AU is the semi-major axis of the earth's orbit and the earth's period is 1 year. Find (a) the semi-major axis of the comet's orbit, (b) its period in years, and (c) the ratio of its speed at perihelion to its speed at aphelion.
questions.a: (a) The semi-major axis is half the distance between perihelion and aphelion: a = (2 + 6)/2 = 4 AU. (b) T^2 is proportional to a^3, so T^2 = 4^3 = 64 and T = 8 years. questions.q: A planet's elliptical orbit has perihelion P and aphelion A at the ends of the major axis, and B and C at the ends of the minor axis; the Sun is at the focus S, which lies between the centre and P. questions.a: No. The area bounded by the path BAC and the lines SB and SC is larger than the area bounded by the path CPB and the same two lines, because S lies on the P side of the minor axis. By the law of areas equal areas are swept in equal times, so the larger area takes longer: the planet takes a longer time to traverse BAC than CPB.
s: Compares the two areas swept from S: the area on the aphelion side (SBAC) is the larger

questions.a: Venus: T^2 = 0.615^2 = 0.378 and a^3 = 10.8^3 = 1260, so T^2/a^3 = 3.00 x 10^-4. Mars: T^2 = 1.88^2 = 3.53 and a^3 = 22.8^3 = 11850, so T^2/a^3 = 2.98 x 10^-4. The two values agree to within about 1 per cent although the planets have very different orbits, which confirms Kepler's law of periods: T^2 is proportional to a^3 with the same constant for all planets.
s: Concludes that the quotient is the same for both, confirming the law of periods

questions.q: A student argues: 'A planet 100 times as far from the Sun as the earth has a path 100 times as long, so it takes 100 years to go round.' Evaluate this claim using Kepler's law of periods.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. T^2 is proportional to a^3, so T^2 = 100^3 = 10^6 and T = 1000 years, not 100. The student has assumed that the distant planet moves as fast as the earth; in fact a planet in a larger orbit also moves more slowly, so the period grows faster than the size of the orbit.
s: Judgement with the correct value: T = 100^(3/2) = 1000 years
Reason: the period is not proportional to the orbit size because the farther planet also moves more slowly (T^2 proportional to a^3)

State the length of string needed between the pins, describe the drawing, and say where on your drawing the Sun must be placed.

Stretch the string taut with the tip of the pencil and move the pencil round, keeping the string taut throughout; the closed curve drawn is the ellipse. The Sun must be placed at one of the two pins (a focus), not at the centre of the ellipse.
s: String length between the pins = 20 cm, justified by the constant sum of distances from the foci
Pins 12 cm apart as foci; pencil keeps the string taut while moving round

concepts.name: The universal law of gravitation, superposition and the gravitational constant
concepts.description: Newton's law for the attraction between two point masses, its vector character, the vector addition of forces from several masses, and Cavendish's torsion-balance measurement of G.
concepts.idea: Every body in the universe attracts every other body; the same force that makes an apple fall keeps the moon in its orbit, and its strength is fixed by one universal constant G that can be measured in the laboratory.
concepts.rule: Every body attracts every other body with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = G m1 m2 / r^2, for point masses. The force is attractive and acts along the line joining the masses; the forces on the two bodies are equal and opposite (F12 = -F21). For a collection of point masses the force on any one is the vector sum of the forces exerted by the others, each acting independently (superposition). Newton's check: the moon's centripetal acceleration 4 pi^2 R_m / T^2 is about g/3600, and the moon is about 60 earth radii away, as an inverse-square force requires. Cavendish (1798): two small lead spheres on a bar hung from a fine wire are attracted by two large spheres; the gravitational torque F x L twists the wire until it equals the restoring torque tau x theta, so G M m L / d^2 = tau theta. The accepted value is G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
concepts.example: Two point masses of 10 kg each placed 1 m apart attract each other with F = 6.67 x 10^-11 x 10 x 10 / 1^2 = 6.67 x 10^-9 N.

Three point masses of 2 kg each are fixed at the vertices A, B and C of an equilateral triangle. A point mass of 1 kg is placed at the centroid O, with OA = OB = OC = 1 m. Take G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2. (a) What is the net gravitational force on the 1 kg mass? (b) The mass at A is now replaced by a 4 kg mass. Find the magnitude, to 3 significant figures, and the direction of the net force on the 1 kg mass.
questions.a: (a) The three forces are equal in magnitude, each G(2)(1)/1^2 = 2G, and are directed towards A, B and C at 120 degrees to one another, so their vector sum is zero. (b) Think of the 4 kg mass as 2 kg + 2 kg: three 2 kg masses give zero net force as before, leaving the force of the extra 2 kg at A. Net force = G(2)(1)/1^2 = 2 x 6.67 x 10^-11 = 1.33 x 10^-10 N, directed from O towards A. (Equivalently, the force towards A is 4G and the forces towards B and C add to 2G directed away from A, giving 4G - 2G = 2G towards A.)
s: (a) Net force is zero: three equal forces at 120 degrees (symmetry)
(b) Resultant 2G directed towards A - either as the extra 2 kg at A acting alone (the symmetric 2 kg set cancels) or as 4G towards A less the 2G that B and C together give away from A
Value 1.33 x 10^-10 N, directed from O towards A

questions.q: Four equal point masses are fixed at the four corners of a square and a small mass is placed at the centre. What is the net gravitational force on the small mass? How does the answer change if one of the corner masses is removed?
questions.a: With all four masses the net force is zero: the masses at opposite corners pull the central mass with equal forces in opposite directions, so each diagonal pair cancels. If one corner mass is removed, the pair on the other diagonal still cancels, and the mass diagonally opposite the empty corner is left unbalanced. The net force then equals the pull of that single mass and is directed from the centre towards it (away from the empty corner).
s: Net force zero with four masses, because the pulls of diagonally opposite masses cancel
With one removed, the net force equals the pull of the opposite corner's mass alone, directed towards that mass

Take pi^2 = 9.87, g = 9.8 m/s^2 at the earth's surface and the earth's radius R_E = 6.4 x 10^6 m. (a) Calculate the moon's centripetal acceleration a_m = 4 pi^2 R_m / T^2, to 3 significant figures. (b) Find the ratio g/a_m to 2 significant figures. (c) Compare it with (R_m/R_E)^2 and state what this shows about the earth's gravitational force.
questions.a: (a) a_m = 4 x 9.87 x 3.84 x 10^8 / (2.36 x 10^6)^2 = 1.516 x 10^10 / 5.57 x 10^12 = 2.72 x 10^-3 m/s^2. (b) g/a_m = 9.8 / (2.72 x 10^-3) = 3.6 x 10^3. (c) R_m/R_E = 3.84 x 10^8 / 6.4 x 10^6 = 60, so (R_m/R_E)^2 = 3600. The two ratios agree: the acceleration produced by the earth falls off as the inverse square of the distance from the earth's centre, which is what led Newton to the universal law of gravitation.
s: (R_m/R_E)^2 = 60^2 = 3600, so the force varies as the inverse square of the distance from the earth's centre

questions.q: To find the gravitational force between a long thin rod and a small ball, a student puts the mass of the rod, the mass of the ball and the distance from the ball to the nearest end of the rod straight into the formula for the universal law of gravitation. Evaluate this method.
questions.a: The method is not valid. The law refers to point masses, and the rod is an extended object. Each small part of the rod is at a different distance from the ball and pulls it in a different direction, so the forces of all the parts have to be added as vectors (in general using calculus). No single distance, and certainly not the distance to the nearest end, can be used in the formula.
s: Judgement: not valid, because the law in this form applies to point masses and the rod is an extended object
Reason: the parts of the rod are at different distances and directions, so their forces must be added vectorially

questions.q: Design the calculation for a Cavendish-type experiment. A light bar of length L = 1.0 m with a small lead sphere of mass m = 0.050 kg at each end hangs from a wire whose restoring torque is tau = 6.67 x 10^-7 N m per radian of twist. Large spheres of mass M = 10 kg are placed so that the centre of each is d = 0.10 m from the centre of its neighbouring small sphere, on opposite sides of the bar, and the bar is observed to turn through theta = 5.0 x 10^-3 rad. Taking the gravitational torque on the bar as F x L, as the chapter does, construct the expression for G and evaluate it.
questions.a: Each large sphere attracts its neighbouring small sphere with F = G M m / d^2, the spheres acting as if their masses were at their centres. The two forces are equal and opposite, so there is no net force on the bar but a torque F x L. At equilibrium this equals the restoring torque of the wire: G M m L / d^2 = tau theta, so G = tau theta d^2 / (M m L). Substituting: G = (6.67 x 10^-7 x 5.0 x 10^-3 x (0.10)^2) / (10 x 0.050 x 1.0) = (3.335 x 10^-11) / 0.50 = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
s: Force between neighbouring spheres F = G M m / d^2 and gravitational torque F x L
Equates to the restoring torque and rearranges: G = tau theta d^2 / (M m L)
Substitutes to get G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2

concepts.name: Spherical shells and the acceleration due to gravity at the earth's surface
concepts.description: The two results for a uniform spherical shell, the earth treated as concentric shells, the force on a mass inside a uniform earth, the expression for g at the surface and its use to estimate the mass of the earth.
concepts.idea: A uniform spherical shell pulls an outside point as if all its mass sat at its centre and does not pull an inside point at all; treating the earth as a nest of such shells gives g in terms of the earth's mass and radius.
concepts.rule: (1) The force of attraction between a hollow spherical shell of uniform density and a point mass situated outside is just as if the entire mass of the shell were concentrated at its centre. (2) The force of attraction due to a hollow spherical shell of uniform density on a point mass situated inside it is zero. The earth can be imagined as concentric shells: at a point outside, the force is as if the whole mass M_E were at the centre. At a distance r from the centre inside a uniform earth, only the sphere of radius r attracts, with mass M_r = M_E r^3 / R_E^3, so F = G m M_r / r^2 = G m M_E r / R_E^3. At the surface F = G M_E m / R_E^2 = m g, so g = G M_E / R_E^2, independent of the mass of the body. With M_E = (4 pi/3) R_E^3 rho, g = (4/3) pi G rho R_E. Knowing g, R_E and G gives M_E = g R_E^2 / G ('Cavendish weighed the earth').

concepts.name: Gravitational potential energy and gravitational potential
concepts.description: Potential energy near the surface (mgh) and at arbitrary distance (-G M m / r with zero at infinity), the potential energy of a system of particles as a sum over pairs, and the gravitational potential as potential energy per unit mass.
concepts.idea: Gravity is a conservative force, so a potential energy can be defined; choosing it to be zero at infinity makes the gravitational potential energy of any two masses a finite distance apart negative.
concepts.rule: Close to the surface the force mg is constant and the potential energy at height h is W(h) = mgh + W_0, so the work done in lifting from h1 to h2 is mg(h2 - h1). At arbitrary distance the force is G M_E m / r^2 and the work done in lifting from r1 to r2 is W_12 = -G M_E m (1/r2 - 1/r1). The potential energy is W(r) = -G M_E m / r + W_1; only differences of potential energy have a definite meaning, and W_1 is conventionally set to zero, so the potential energy at a point is the work done in displacing the particle from infinity to that point. For two particles, V = -G m1 m2 / r (zero at infinity). An isolated system of particles has total potential energy equal to the sum over all possible pairs. The gravitational potential at a point is the potential energy of a particle of unit mass at that point: -G M / r for a mass M, in J/kg, a scalar. Potential energy is in joule.
concepts.example: Two point masses of 3 kg and 5 kg placed 0.5 m apart have potential energy V = -G x 3 x 5 / 0.5 = -30 G = -2.0 x 10^-9 J (zero at infinity, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2).

Take G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2, sqrt(2) = 1.414 and the zero of potential energy and of potential at infinity. Find, to 3 significant figures, (a) the gravitational potential energy of the system and (b) the gravitational potential at the centre of the square.
questions.a: (a) There are 6 pairs: 4 pairs along the sides at distance 1 m and 2 pairs along the diagonals at distance sqrt(2) m. Potential energy = -4 G m^2 / l - 2 G m^2 / (sqrt(2) l) = -(G m^2 / l)(4 + 1.414) = -5.414 x 6.67 x 10^-11 x 4 = -1.44 x 10^-9 J. (b) Each mass is at a distance l / sqrt(2) = 0.707 m from the centre, so the potential = -4 G m / (l / sqrt(2)) = -4 x 1.414 x 6.67 x 10^-11 x 2 = -7.55 x 10^-10 J/kg.

Potential energy = -1.44 x 10^-9 J

questions.q: For the difference in the potential energy of a body of mass m between two points at distances r1 and r2 from the centre of the earth (mass M), two expressions are offered: -G M m (1/r2 - 1/r1) and m g (r2 - r1). Evaluate which is the more accurate and why.

The expression m g (r2 - r1) takes the force to be the constant mg, which is only practically true close to the earth's surface, at heights much smaller than the earth's radius; it is an approximation to the first expression.

Reason: m g (r2 - r1) assumes a constant force and holds only near the surface, whereas the force actually varies as 1/r^2

questions.q: Design a system of three unequal point masses placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 2 m. Choose the masses, then write the gravitational potential energy of each pair and of the whole system in terms of G (zero at infinity), give the total in joule to 3 significant figures using G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2, and state the work an external agent must do to separate the three masses to infinity.

(Any three unequal masses are acceptable, with the total equal to minus G times the sum of the three products of masses divided by 2 m.)
s: Chooses three unequal masses and writes -G m1 m2 / r for each of the three pairs with r = 2 m
Adds the three pair energies to get the (negative) total, evaluated in joule
Work to separate to infinity equals the magnitude of the total potential energy, and is positive

concepts.name: Escape speed
concepts.description: Using conservation of energy to find the minimum speed with which a body must be projected to reach infinity, the expressions sqrt(2 G M_E / R_E) and sqrt(2 g R_E), their value for the earth and the moon, and motion between two fixed spheres through a neutral point.
concepts.idea: A body thrown fast enough never comes back: if its kinetic energy at launch is at least equal to the magnitude of its (negative) gravitational potential energy, it can reach infinity.
concepts.rule: For a body of mass m projected with speed V_i from a distance (h + R_E) from the earth's centre, conservation of energy gives m V_i^2 / 2 - G m M_E / (h + R_E) = m V_f^2 / 2, where V_f is the speed at infinity. The right side is at least zero, so the minimum speed satisfies m V_i^2 / 2 = G m M_E / (h + R_E). From the surface (h = 0): escape speed = sqrt(2 G M_E / R_E) = sqrt(2 g R_E), about 11.2 km/s for the earth. The mass m cancels. For the moon the escape speed is about 2.3 km/s, about five times smaller, which is why the moon has no atmosphere. Between two fixed spheres there is a neutral point where their attractions cancel; a projectile need only reach it, after which the other sphere's pull suffices.
concepts.example: For a body of radius 2.0 x 10^6 m on whose surface the acceleration due to gravity is 1.0 m/s^2, the escape speed is sqrt(2 x 1.0 x 2.0 x 10^6) = 2.0 x 10^3 m/s = 2.0 km/s.

questions.q: The escape speed from the earth's surface is 11.2 km/s. A body is projected from the surface with twice this speed. Ignoring the Sun, other planets and air resistance, find its speed when it is far away from the earth. Take sqrt(3) = 1.732 and give the answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.a: Let v_e be the escape speed, so (1/2) m v_e^2 = G M_E m / R_E. Conservation of energy between the surface and infinity: (1/2) m (2 v_e)^2 - G M_E m / R_E = (1/2) m v_f^2, that is (1/2) m (4 v_e^2) - (1/2) m v_e^2 = (1/2) m v_f^2. So v_f^2 = 3 v_e^2 and v_f = sqrt(3) x 11.2 = 19.4 km/s.
s: Applies conservation of energy, replacing G M_E m / R_E by (1/2) m v_e^2, to get v_f^2 = 4 v_e^2 - v_e^2
v_f = sqrt(3) x 11.2 = 19.4 km/s

With v^2 = g R_E and G M_E = g R_E^2: (1/2) g R_E - g R_E = -g R_E^2 / r, so g R_E / 2 = g R_E^2 / r and r = 2 R_E. The height above the surface is r - R_E = R_E = 6400 km.
s: Writes conservation of energy with potential energy -G M_E m / r and zero speed at the highest point
Substitutes v^2 = g R_E and G M_E = g R_E^2 to get r = 2 R_E from the centre

questions.q: Two uniform spheres of masses M and 4M are held fixed with their centres 6R apart. The point N on the line of centres, at a distance 2R from the centre of the sphere of mass M, is where their attractions on a particle cancel. A projectile is fired from the surface of the lighter sphere directly towards the heavier one. Explain why the minimum speed of projection is the one that just takes the projectile to N, and what its speed at N is in that case.
questions.a: Between the lighter sphere and N the net force on the projectile is back towards the lighter sphere, so the projectile slows down; beyond N the pull of the heavier sphere is the greater, so the net force is towards the heavier sphere and carries the projectile the rest of the way without any further speed being needed. Hence it is sufficient to project it with a speed that just enables it to reach N. For this minimum speed the projectile's speed at N approaches zero, so its mechanical energy there is purely potential.
s: Explains that the net force reverses at N: beyond N the heavier sphere's greater pull takes the projectile onward
States that for the minimum speed of projection the speed at N approaches zero

questions.q: Two uniform spheres, each of radius R, have masses M and 9M and are held fixed with their centres 8R apart. A projectile of mass m is fired from the surface of the sphere of mass M directly towards the centre of the other sphere. Obtain, in terms of G, M and R, the minimum speed of projection for it to reach the surface of the second sphere.
questions.a: Neutral point N at distance r from the centre of M: G M m / r^2 = G (9M) m / (8R - r)^2, so 8R - r = 3r and r = 2R (6R from the centre of 9M). The projectile must just reach N. At the surface of M it is R from one centre and 7R from the other: E_i = (1/2) m v^2 - G M m / R - 9 G M m / (7R). At N with zero speed: E_N = -G M m / (2R) - 9 G M m / (6R) = -2 G M m / R. Equating: (1/2) v^2 = G M / R + 9 G M / (7R) - 2 G M / R = 2 G M / (7R). Hence v^2 = 4 G M / (7R) and v = sqrt(4 G M / (7R)) = 2 sqrt(G M / (7R)).
s: Locates the neutral point at 2R from the centre of the sphere of mass M
Writes the energy at the surface (distances R and 7R) and at N (distances 2R and 6R, zero speed)
Equates them to get v = sqrt(4 G M / (7R))

questions.q: A student makes two claims about launching a body so that it escapes from the earth: (i) a heavier body needs a greater speed of projection than a lighter one, and (ii) the body escapes only if it is projected vertically upwards. Evaluate both claims using the way the escape speed is derived (neglect air resistance).
questions.a: Both claims are wrong. (i) In the energy equation (1/2) m V^2 = G m M_E / (h + R_E) the mass m of the body cancels, so the escape speed is the same for all bodies. (ii) The condition is derived from conservation of energy, and kinetic energy depends only on the speed, not on the direction of the velocity, so the escape speed does not depend on the direction of projection.
s: (i) Wrong: the mass of the body cancels from the energy equation
(ii) Wrong: the energy condition involves only the speed, so the direction of projection does not matter

questions.q: An astronaut stands on a small spherical asteroid of radius 2000 m on whose surface the acceleration due to gravity is 1.0 x 10^-3 m/s^2. Her jumping speed of 3.0 m/s is greater than this, so she would escape and never return. Conservation of energy with (1/2) m v_e^2 = G M m / R gives v_f^2 = v^2 - v_e^2 = 9.0 - 4.0 = 5.0, so far away her speed would be sqrt(5) = 2.2 m/s. She should therefore not jump at full strength (a safe jump must be slower than 2.0 m/s).
s: Escape speed = sqrt(2 g R) = 2.0 m/s
Decision: 3.0 m/s exceeds 2.0 m/s, so she escapes
Speed far away = sqrt(3.0^2 - 2.0^2) = 2.2 m/s by conservation of energy

concepts.name: Earth satellites: orbital speed and time period
concepts.description: A satellite in a circular orbit with gravity as the centripetal force: its speed, its period, Kepler's law of periods for satellites, the period of a satellite close to the surface, and finding the mass of the central body from an orbit.
concepts.idea: A satellite stays in a circular orbit because the earth's gravitational pull supplies exactly the centripetal force its speed requires; this fixes both the speed and the period for each orbital radius.
concepts.rule: Earth satellites obey Kepler's laws; their orbits are circular or elliptic, and the moon is the only natural satellite, with a period of about 27.3 days. For a circular orbit at distance (R_E + h) from the earth's centre, m V^2 / (R_E + h) = G m M_E / (R_E + h)^2, so V^2 = G M_E / (R_E + h): V decreases as h increases and does not involve m. For h = 0, V^2 = G M_E / R_E = g R_E. The period is T = 2 pi (R_E + h) / V = 2 pi (R_E + h)^(3/2) / sqrt(G M_E), so T^2 = k (R_E + h)^3 with k = 4 pi^2 / (G M_E): Kepler's law of periods for satellites of the earth. For a satellite very close to the surface T_0 = 2 pi sqrt(R_E / g), about 85 minutes. For elliptical orbits (R_E + h) is replaced by the semi-major axis, with the earth at one focus. The same relation gives the mass of any central body: M = 4 pi^2 R^3 / (G T^2).
concepts.example: A satellite in a circular orbit of radius 16 R_E (measured from the earth's centre) has a speed sqrt(g R_E / 16), one-quarter of the speed of a satellite close to the surface, and a period 16^(3/2) = 64 times T_0.

To shorten the period the satellite must be put in a lower orbit; the shortest possible period is that of a satellite close to the surface, about 85 minutes.

The orbital radius is 3.84 x 10^5 / 4 = 9.6 x 10^4 km from the earth's centre. The height above the surface is 96000 - 6400 = 89600 km (about 9.0 x 10^4 km).

concepts.name: Energy of an orbiting satellite
concepts.description: Kinetic, potential and total energy of a satellite in a circular orbit, the relations among them, why the total energy of a bound satellite is negative, and the energy needed to change orbit or to escape.
concepts.idea: A satellite in orbit has positive kinetic energy and negative potential energy of twice the size, so its total energy is negative: it is bound to the earth.
concepts.rule: For a satellite of mass m in a circular orbit at distance (R_E + h) from the earth's centre: kinetic energy K.E. = G m M_E / (2 (R_E + h)); potential energy (zero at infinity) P.E. = -G m M_E / (R_E + h); total energy E = K.E. + P.E. = -G m M_E / (2 (R_E + h)). So the K.E. is positive and half the magnitude of the P.E., E = -K.E. = P.E./2, and E is negative. In an elliptic orbit K.E. and P.E. vary from point to point but the total energy stays constant and negative. If the total energy were positive or zero the object would escape to infinity; satellites are at finite distance, so their energies cannot be positive or zero. Moving to a larger orbit raises the total energy (less negative), lowers the kinetic energy by the same amount and raises the potential energy by twice that amount.
concepts.example: A satellite whose kinetic energy in a circular orbit is 3 x 10^9 J has potential energy -6 x 10^9 J and total energy -3 x 10^9 J (zero of potential energy at infinity).

A satellite of mass 500 kg moves in a circular orbit at a height of 1600 km above the earth's surface. Take the earth's radius as 6.4 x 10^6 m, the earth's mass as 6.0 x 10^24 kg and G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2. How much energy must be supplied to take the satellite out of the earth's gravitational influence? Give the answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.a: The orbital radius is r = 6.4 x 10^6 + 1.6 x 10^6 = 8.0 x 10^6 m. The total energy in orbit is E = -G M_E m / (2r). To escape, the total energy must be raised to zero, so the energy needed = G M_E m / (2r) = 6.67 x 10^-11 x 6.0 x 10^24 x 500 / (2 x 8.0 x 10^6) = 1.25 x 10^10 J.

questions.q: A 200 kg satellite is in a circular orbit of radius 2 R_E about the earth, measured from the earth's centre. It is to be transferred to a circular orbit of radius 3 R_E. Take g = 9.8 m/s^2, R_E = 6.4 x 10^6 m and use G M_E = g R_E^2, with the zero of potential energy at infinity. Find, to 3 significant figures, (a) the energy required, (b) the change in the kinetic energy and (c) the change in the potential energy, giving the sign of each change.
questions.a: Total energy in a circular orbit of radius r is E = -G M_E m / (2r). Initially E_i = -G M_E m / (4 R_E); finally E_f = -G M_E m / (6 R_E). (a) Energy required = E_f - E_i = G M_E m / (12 R_E) = g m R_E / 12 = 9.8 x 200 x 6.4 x 10^6 / 12 = 1.05 x 10^9 J. (b) K.E. = -E, so the change in kinetic energy = -1.05 x 10^9 J (it decreases). (c) P.E. = 2E, so the change in potential energy = +2.09 x 10^9 J (it increases, becoming less negative).
s: Energy required = E_f - E_i = G M_E m / (12 R_E) = g m R_E / 12 = 1.05 x 10^9 J
Change in kinetic energy = -1.05 x 10^9 J (decrease)
Change in potential energy = +2.09 x 10^9 J (increase)

questions.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at a distance r from the centre of the earth, and an object of the same mass is held at rest at the same distance r. Compare the energies that must be supplied to each to take it out of the earth's gravitational influence, and explain the difference.
questions.a: The object at rest has only potential energy -G M_E m / r, so it needs G M_E m / r to bring its total energy up to zero. The orbiting satellite also has kinetic energy G M_E m / (2r), so its total energy is -G M_E m / (2r) and it needs only G M_E m / (2r). The satellite therefore needs less energy, exactly half as much, because it already possesses kinetic energy equal to half the magnitude of its potential energy.
s: Object at rest needs G M_E m / r; orbiting satellite needs G M_E m / (2r)
Explains that the satellite needs half as much because of the kinetic energy it already has

questions.q: A satellite of mass m moves with speed v in a circular orbit of radius r, measured from the centre of the earth of mass M_E. Starting from the condition that gravity provides the centripetal force, derive expressions for its kinetic energy, its potential energy (zero at infinity) and its total energy, and state what the sign of the total energy tells us.
questions.a: Centripetal force = gravitational force: m v^2 / r = G m M_E / r^2, so v^2 = G M_E / r and the kinetic energy = (1/2) m v^2 = G m M_E / (2r). The potential energy at distance r, taking it as zero at infinity, is -G m M_E / r. Total energy E = G m M_E / (2r) - G m M_E / r = -G m M_E / (2r). The total energy is negative, which shows that the satellite is bound to the earth: it cannot reach infinity unless energy of at least G m M_E / (2r) is supplied.
s: From m v^2 / r = G m M_E / r^2, kinetic energy = G m M_E / (2r)
Potential energy = -G m M_E / r
Total energy = -G m M_E / (2r); negative sign means the satellite is bound

questions.q: A satellite in a low circular orbit slowly loses energy because of the thin upper atmosphere, its orbit remaining nearly circular. A student concludes: 'It is losing energy, so it must be slowing down.' Evaluate this conclusion using the energy relations for a circular orbit.
questions.a: The conclusion is wrong. Losing energy makes the total energy more negative; since E = -G m M_E / (2r), the orbital radius r must become smaller. The kinetic energy equals -E, so as E becomes more negative the kinetic energy increases: the satellite moves into a lower orbit and speeds up. The potential energy falls by twice the amount the kinetic energy rises, which accounts for the energy lost.
s: Judgement: wrong; a more negative total energy means a smaller orbital radius
Kinetic energy = -E increases, so the satellite speeds up

questions.q: Construct an energy table for a 1000 kg satellite in circular orbits of radius 4 R_E and 8 R_E, measured from the earth's centre. Take g = 9.8 m/s^2, R_E = 6.4 x 10^6 m and use G M_E = g R_E^2, with the zero of potential energy at infinity. For each orbit give the kinetic energy, the potential energy and the total energy to 3 significant figures, and then state the energy needed to transfer the satellite from the smaller orbit to the larger one.
questions.a: G M_E m / R_E = g m R_E = 9.8 x 1000 x 6.4 x 10^6 = 6.272 x 10^10 J. For a circular orbit of radius r: K.E. = G M_E m / (2r), P.E. = -G M_E m / r, E = -G M_E m / (2r). Orbit of radius 4 R_E: K.E. = 6.272 x 10^10 / 8 = 7.84 x 10^9 J, P.E. = -1.57 x 10^10 J, E = -7.84 x 10^9 J. Orbit of radius 8 R_E: K.E. = 6.272 x 10^10 / 16 = 3.92 x 10^9 J, P.E. = -7.84 x 10^9 J, E = -3.92 x 10^9 J. Energy needed for the transfer = E(8 R_E) - E(4 R_E) = -3.92 x 10^9 - (-7.84 x 10^9) = 3.92 x 10^9 J.
s: Energy for the transfer = difference of total energies = 3.92 x 10^9 J
